record.paper_title: Channel Training & Estimation for Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces: Exposition of Principles, Approaches, and Open Problems
record.original_question: Is perfect deactivation of RIS elements physically feasible for communication systems that need to suppress all RIS reflections during channel estimation, and if so, what electromagnetic design conditions and implementation methods make that feasible in a conclusive and communication-relevant way?

evidence.quote: the question of its physical feasibility remains unresolved.

To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no currently-available study in the open literature offers an in-depth and conclusive treatment of the feasibility of perfect deactivation of RIS elements and related design issues.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS), modeled as a planar array of N sub-wavelength scattering elements, each loaded with a tunable impedance that determines a complex reflection coefficient r_n ∈ ℂ. In a typical wireless communication setting, an RIS is placed in the propagation environment between a transmitter and a receiver, so that the receiver observes a superposition of (i) the direct (non-RIS) channel and (ii) the cascaded channel through the RIS, whose contribution depends linearly on the reflection coefficients {r_n}. For training and channel estimation, one often wishes to "deactivate" the RIS — meaning to choose impedance loads so that, when illuminated by an incident electromagnetic wave at the carrier frequency of interest, the RIS contributes no scattered field to the receiver, i.e. effectively r_n = 0 for every element n. Call this condition "perfect deactivation" of the RIS.

Formulate and resolve the following:

(a) Is perfect deactivation of every RIS element physically realizable, in the sense that there exist passive (or otherwise implementable) load impedances Z_n such that, accounting for mutual coupling between elements, the total scattered field produced by the RIS in response to an arbitrary incident plane wave at the operating frequency vanishes identically in the far field (or, more weakly, vanishes at the receiver location relevant to a communication link)?

(b) If perfect deactivation is feasible, specify the electromagnetic design conditions (load impedance values, element geometry, inter-element spacing, mutual-coupling constraints, bandwidth, polarization, angle-of-arrival dependence) and the implementation methods (e.g., open-circuit loads, matched loads, absorbing loads, switched terminations) under which it can be achieved in a conclusive and communication-relevant manner.

(c) If perfect deactivation is not feasible, quantify the minimum achievable residual reflected power and characterize the fundamental physical obstructions (e.g., structural scattering from the metallic backplane and element bodies, mutual coupling, finite-Q resonances) that prevent it.
artifact.status_search_result: A web search did not surface any conclusive, in-depth electromagnetic study establishing perfect deactivation of RIS elements as physically realizable in a communication-relevant sense. Existing channel-estimation schemes commonly assume an idealized on/off capability for RIS elements, while practical works note structural-scattering and mutual-coupling limitations that prevent truly zero reflection. The question therefore appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Channel Estimation for RIS Assisted Wireless Communications
status_evidence.snippet: Assumes each RIS element can be turned on/off with arbitrary phase in the on state, used as an idealization for estimation.
status_evidence.claim: On/off RIS element control is typically assumed as an idealized capability rather than electromagnetically verified.

status_evidence.title: An Overview of Signal Processing Techniques for RIS/IRS-aided Wireless Systems
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses selective activation patterns and limitations of active components in RIS, indicating practical constraints on full deactivation.
status_evidence.claim: Practical RIS architectures impose limits on truly turning off elements; full feasibility of perfect deactivation is not conclusively established.
